author: A Robot
objectives: Determine the steric number of a central atom from its Lewis structure by counting bonding pairs and lone pairs.
Predict the electron-domain geometry of a molecule from its steric number (linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, or octahedral).
Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry, and identify molecular shapes produced when lone pairs are present.
Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs and predict resulting bond-angle deviations.
Apply VSEPR predictions to real molecules and compare them to experimentally observed structures.

modules.moduleName: Foundations of VSEPR: Electron Domains and Repulsion
modules.description: Introduces the core principle of VSEPR theory: electron domains around a central atom arrange to minimize repulsion. Students see how counting bonding and lone pairs gives the steric number.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Define electron domains as regions of electron density (bonds or lone pairs) around a central atom.
Determine the steric number of a central atom from a Lewis structure.
Understand the central postulate that electron domains arrange to minimize mutual repulsion.
instructions: Observe the central atom and surrounding electron domains as they appear.
Listen for how the steric number is determined by counting bonding pairs and lone pairs.

clips.changeMeaning: Initial staging: central atom and two electron domains appear, establishing the basic VSEPR setup before any interaction.
clips.narration: VSEPR theory, short for Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion, predicts molecular shape based on a simple idea: electron pairs around a central atom repel each other and will arrange themselves in space to be as far apart as possible. Here we see a central atom with two electron domains nearby.

clips.changeMeaning: A text label appears above the central atom displaying the steric number, reinforcing the counting concept just narrated.
clips.narration: Each region of electron density around the central atom - whether it's a bonding pair shared with another atom, or a lone pair belonging only to the central atom - counts as one electron domain. Adding up all these domains gives us the steric number. Here, with two domains, our steric number is two.

clips.changeMeaning: The two electron domains animate outward to opposite sides of the central atom, visually demonstrating repulsion minimization resulting in a linear arrangement at 180 degrees.
clips.narration: Because these electron domains are all negatively charged, they repel one another. To minimize this repulsion, they push apart to the maximum possible angle. With only two domains, that means settling at exactly opposite sides of the central atom - 180 degrees apart. This gives us our first electron-domain geometry: linear.

modules.description: Walks through the five fundamental electron-domain geometries produced by steric numbers 2 through 6: linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the electron-domain geometry associated with each steric number from 2 to 6.
Visualize the spatial arrangement of 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 electron domains that minimizes repulsion.
Recognize the idealized bond angles associated with each geometry (180°, 120°, 109.5°, 90°/120°, 90°).
instructions: Watch as electron domains are added one at a time around the central atom.
Note how the geometry changes shape and idealized bond angles as domains increase.

clips.changeMeaning: A third electron domain (d3) is enabled and the existing two domains reposition into a trigonal planar arrangement at 120 degree angles, updating the label accordingly.
clips.narration: Let's add a third electron domain. To keep maximum distance from its neighbors, the three domains spread out in a single plane, 120 degrees apart from each other. This is the trigonal planar geometry - the arrangement for steric number 3.

clips.changeMeaning: A fourth domain (d4) is enabled and all four domains reposition into a tetrahedral arrangement, demonstrating the 3D geometry for steric number 4.
clips.narration: Now let's add a fourth domain. In three dimensions, four domains achieve maximum separation by pointing toward the corners of a tetrahedron, with bond angles of 109.5 degrees. This tetrahedral geometry is extremely common - it's the shape adopted by carbon in methane.

clips.changeMeaning: A fifth domain (d5) is enabled; domains reposition into a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement with three equatorial and two axial positions, illustrating the mixed 90/120 degree geometry.
clips.narration: With five domains, a single uniform angle is no longer possible. Instead, three domains form an equatorial triangle at 120 degrees, while two more occupy axial positions above and below at 90 degrees to the equator. This is the trigonal bipyramidal geometry, seen in molecules like PF5.

clips.changeMeaning: A sixth domain (d6) is enabled and all six domains reposition into an octahedral arrangement, completing the survey of the five fundamental electron-domain geometries.
clips.narration: Finally, with six domains, the most symmetric arrangement is octahedral: four domains form a square around the central atom, with one more above and one below, all at 90 degree angles to their neighbors. This is the geometry seen in molecules like SF6.

modules.moduleName: Lone Pairs and Molecular Geometry: Water and Ammonia
modules.description: Explores how lone pairs modify the observed molecular shape within a tetrahedral electron-domain geometry, producing bent and trigonal pyramidal shapes, and explains why lone pairs cause bond angles to compress.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry.
Identify bent and trigonal pyramidal shapes as tetrahedral-derived geometries with lone pairs.
Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, and predict resulting bond-angle compression.
instructions: Compare the electron-domain arrangement to the visible molecular shape once lone pairs are highlighted.
Notice the bond angle change as lone pairs are introduced.

components.text: Lone pairs are 'fatter' - they push bonding pairs closer together

clips.changeMeaning: The water molecule model appears with its four electron domains in a tetrahedral arrangement, setting up the distinction between electron-domain and molecular geometry.
clips.narration: Water's central oxygen atom has a steric number of 4: two bonding pairs to hydrogen, and two lone pairs. The electron-domain geometry is tetrahedral, just like methane. But watch what happens to the visible molecular shape when we only look at the atoms.

clips.changeMeaning: The angle label updates to show the observed bent geometry and compressed bond angle, and the explanatory label about lone pair spatial dominance appears.
clips.narration: When we hide the lone pairs and look only at where the atoms are, water's molecular shape is bent - not tetrahedral. The two lone pairs are still there, still repelling, but they're invisible in the final molecular shape. Because lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, they compress the H-O-H bond angle down from the ideal 109.5 degrees to about 104.5 degrees.

components.text: More lone pairs = more compression: H2O (104.5°) vs NH3 (107°) vs CH4 (109.5°)

clips.changeMeaning: The ammonia molecule model appears alongside water for direct comparison, illustrating how the number of lone pairs determines the degree of bond angle compression and resulting shape.
clips.narration: Ammonia shows a similar effect with only one lone pair. Nitrogen's steric number is also 4 - tetrahedral electron-domain geometry - but with three bonding pairs and one lone pair, the resulting molecular shape is trigonal pyramidal. The single lone pair still compresses the H-N-H angle, but less severely than water's two lone pairs - down to about 107 degrees instead of 109.5.

modules.moduleName: Beyond Tetrahedral: Seesaw, T-Shaped, Square Planar, and Square Pyramidal
modules.description: Extends the lone-pair-substitution concept to the trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral electron-domain geometries, producing seesaw, T-shaped, square pyramidal, and square planar molecular shapes, matched against real molecules.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify seesaw and T-shaped geometries as trigonal-bipyramidal-derived shapes with one or two lone pairs.
Identify square pyramidal and square planar geometries as octahedral-derived shapes with one or two lone pairs.
Apply VSEPR predictions to PF5, SF4 (implied), XeF4, and SF6 and compare to experimentally observed structures.
instructions: Observe how replacing bonding domains with lone pairs on the trigonal bipyramid and octahedron changes the resulting molecular shape.
Compare each predicted shape to its real molecule example.

clips.changeMeaning: PF5 model is shown as the baseline trigonal bipyramidal reference with zero lone pairs, establishing the starting geometry before lone pair substitutions are discussed conceptually.
clips.narration: Starting from the trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry, replacing one equatorial bonding pair with a lone pair gives the seesaw shape, as seen in sulfur tetrafluoride. Replace two equatorial positions with lone pairs, and the remaining three bonding pairs form a T-shape. In both cases, lone pairs preferentially occupy equatorial positions, where they experience less crowding at 90 degrees from fewer neighbors.

components.text: XeF4: Square Planar (octahedral e-domain, 2 lone pairs)

clips.changeMeaning: XeF4 model is enabled and displayed, demonstrating how two lone pairs positioned opposite each other in an octahedral framework produce a square planar molecular shape.
clips.narration: Now consider the octahedral electron-domain geometry with six domains. In xenon tetrafluoride, XeF4, the central xenon has four bonding pairs and two lone pairs. To minimize repulsion, the two lone pairs occupy positions directly opposite each other - axial positions - leaving the four fluorine atoms arranged in a perfect square around the xenon. This produces the square planar molecular geometry.

components.text: SF6: Octahedral (0 lone pairs) - matches e-domain geometry exactly

clips.changeMeaning: SF6 model is enabled to complete the comparison set, showing a case where molecular geometry equals electron-domain geometry due to the absence of lone pairs.
clips.narration: Finally, sulfur hexafluoride, SF6, has six bonding pairs and zero lone pairs around its central sulfur atom. With no lone pairs to modify the shape, the molecular geometry matches the electron-domain geometry exactly: a perfect octahedron. This confirms our VSEPR prediction against the experimentally observed structure of SF6.
